13314.heading: Element Load Vector
13314.content:
An element load vector collects the external influences assigned to an element's nodes. It can represent concentrated nodal forces, equivalent loads from a distributed source, thermal loading, or another problem-specific excitation.

Distributed effects are converted through the element interpolation so they are work-equivalent to nodal quantities. During assembly, element load contributions sharing a global degree of freedom are summed.

13317.title: Element Order
13317.heading: Element Order
13317.content:
The order of a group element is the least positive integer n for which aⁿ equals the identity, when such an integer exists. It is also the size of the cyclic subgroup generated by the element.

In a finite group, element order divides group order.

13320.heading: Element Nodes in Thermal Models
13320.content:
Finite elements meet at nodes where the numerical solution represents temperature degrees of freedom. One-dimensional elements connect endpoints, two-dimensional elements cover areas, and three-dimensional elements fill volumes while sharing nodes with their neighbors.

Conservation and constitutive relations assembled over all elements couple those nodal unknowns into a global system. More nodes can represent finer variation, but they also increase solution cost, so [[Thermal Mesh Refinement|mesh density]] should follow the physics rather than be uniform by habit.

13323.heading: Electrostatic Poisson Finite Element Problem
13323.content:
An electrostatic Poisson finite element problem solves scalar potential in a region containing prescribed volume charge. Linear triangular elements approximate both the potential and source distribution at their nodes.

The assembled equation contains a field-gradient matrix and a source-weighting matrix. Prescribed potentials partition free and fixed nodes, after which iterative or band-matrix solution yields the unknown potential values.

13326.heading: Element Heat Conductivity Matrix
13326.content:
An element heat conductivity matrix relates nodal temperatures to conductive heat-flow rates. For a uniform one-dimensional element, it scales with conductivity and area and inversely with element length.

Its signed two-node pattern mirrors the axial-bar stiffness matrix because both govern a gradient-driven flux. Assembly combines elements of different materials into a global conduction system.

13329.title: Electrostatic Field
13329.heading: Electrostatic Field
13329.content:
An electrostatic field is a time-independent electric field produced by stationary charge. Its curl is zero, so it can be represented as the negative gradient of a scalar electric potential.

Gauss's law and material permittivity determine how charge shapes the field. The potential satisfies Poisson's equation in charged regions and Laplace's equation where volume charge is absent.

13332.content:
Electronic word of mouth is the online exchange of opinions and experiences about products, services, organizations, or events. Reviews and recommendations can spread beyond direct acquaintances and strongly influence later decisions.

The influence attracts manipulation through fake reviews, coordinated promotion, or malicious criticism. Credibility depends on evidence about contributors, relationships, timing, and patterns of behavior.

13335.title: Electronics Miniaturization
13335.heading: Electronics Miniaturization
13335.content:
Electronics miniaturization reduces the size, weight, and power demands of circuits while increasing functional density. Hearing aids, proximity fuses, missiles, and spacecraft created strong early demand for compact components.

Miniaturization changed system possibilities as well as packaging. Smaller reliable circuits could be embedded in places where room-sized computing equipment was impossible.

13338.sourceSearchName: electron energy band electron energy band
13338.title: Electron Energy Band
13338.heading: Electron Energy Band
13338.content: When many atoms form a crystalline solid, interactions spread their individual electron energy levels into bands of allowed states. The upper occupied band is the valence band; the next available band is the conduction band. Their occupancy and separation explain why a material conducts readily, acts as an insulator, or needs excitation to conduct as a semiconductor. See [[Semiconductor Band Gap]].

13341.title: Electronic Circuits
13341.heading: Electronic Circuits
13341.content:
A combinatorial logic circuit connects AND, OR, and NOT gates without feedback loops. Each wire carries one of two states, interpreted as true and false or as one and zero, and each output wire represents a [[Compound Propositions|compound proposition]] in the circuit's inputs.

[[Boolean Algebra]] can replace that proposition with a simpler equivalent formula and thereby reduce the number of required gates. Circuits with feedback are different because they can store state and do not correspond to a single acyclic proposition.

13344.title: Electron Diffraction
13344.heading: Electron Diffraction
13344.content: Electron diffraction occurs when electrons pass through a crystal or aperture with structure comparable to their [[de Broglie Wavelength]]. The resulting interference pattern demonstrates that matter propagates with wave-like probability amplitudes. Changing accelerating voltage changes electron momentum and therefore the diffraction spacing.

13346.heading: Document

13347.sourceSearchName: electromagnetic continuity equation electromagnetic continuity equation
13347.title: Electromagnetic Continuity Equation
13347.heading: Electromagnetic Continuity Equation
13347.content:
The electromagnetic continuity equation expresses conservation of electric charge. The divergence of current density equals the negative time rate of change of volume charge density.

In steady or quasi-static conditions where charge does not accumulate, current density is divergence-free. The equation is implicit in Maxwell's equations and constrains physically valid source distributions.

13350.sourceSearchName: electromagnetic boundary condition electromagnetic boundary condition
13350.title: Electromagnetic Boundary Condition
13350.heading: Electromagnetic Boundary Condition
13350.content:
An electromagnetic boundary condition specifies how field components behave across an interface between materials. Maxwell's integral laws determine continuity or jumps in tangential electric and magnetic fields and normal electric and magnetic fluxes.

Surface charge and surface current create specific discontinuities. Perfect conductors impose stronger conditions, including zero internal electric field, that shape the neighboring solution.

13351.title: Electromagnetic Boundary Condition

13353.title: Electrical Resistance
13353.heading: Electrical Resistance
13353.content: Electrical resistance is the ratio $R=V/I$ for a component at a specified operating condition. An ohmic conductor has a linear current-voltage relation with constant resistance. For a uniform wire, $R=\rho L/A$, linking resistance to material resistivity, length, and cross-sectional area. Temperature can change resistivity and invalidate a constant-$R$ approximation.

13355.sourceSearchName: electromagnetic constitutive relation electromagnetic constitutive relation
13355.title: Electromagnetic Constitutive Relation
13355.heading: Document

13356.sourceSearchName: electromagnetic constitutive relation electromagnetic constitutive relation
13356.title: Electromagnetic Constitutive Relation
13356.heading: Electromagnetic Constitutive Relation
13356.content:
An electromagnetic constitutive relation connects field quantities through material properties. Permittivity relates electric displacement to electric field, permeability relates magnetic flux to magnetic field, and conductivity relates current density to electric field.

The relations may be linear or nonlinear, isotropic or anisotropic, and homogeneous or position dependent. Maxwell's equations cannot determine a material-specific field without these properties.

13362.title: Electrical Power
13362.heading: Electrical Power
13362.content: Electrical power is the rate of electrical energy transfer, $P=VI$. For an ohmic resistor, substitution gives $P=I^2R=V^2/R$. A real source's internal resistance dissipates some power inside the source, so its terminal voltage and delivered load power depend on current.

13365.title: Electrical Impedance
13365.heading: Electrical Impedance
13365.content: Electrical impedance combines resistance and reactance into the complex ratio of AC voltage to current. Its magnitude determines current amplitude, while its phase determines the offset between current and voltage. In a series RLC circuit, $|Z|=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$, with resonance when inductive and capacitive reactances cancel.

13368.sourceSearchName: electric power transmission loss electric power transmission loss
13368.title: Electric Power Transmission Loss
13368.heading: Electric Power Transmission Loss
13368.content: Centralized electricity generation must deliver output through transmission and distribution infrastructure before users receive it. Line resistance, voltage drop, outages, and construction or maintenance costs reduce the practical value of power produced at the plant. The source contrasts this with [[Captive Power Plant]] and [[Autonomous Power Plant]] arrangements that generate near demand. Avoiding transmission does not remove losses inside the local plant.

13371.sourceSearchName: electric field strength electric field strength
13371.title: Electric Field Strength
13371.heading: Electric Field Strength
13371.content: Electric field strength at a point is the force per unit positive test charge, $E=F/q$. It is a vector whose direction is the force direction for a positive charge. For a point source charge, $E=(1/4\pi\varepsilon_0)Q/r^2$, directed radially outward for positive $Q$ and inward for negative $Q$.

13372.title: Electric Field Strength

13374.title: Electric Potential
13374.heading: Electric Potential
13374.content: Electric potential is electric potential energy per unit positive charge. Potential difference is the work done per unit charge in moving between two points, $V=\Delta U/q$. It is a scalar, so potentials from several source charges add algebraically. The electric field points in the direction of decreasing potential.

13377.title: Electric Motor
13377.heading: Electric Motor
13377.content: An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical rotation. Opposite sides of a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experience forces that form a torque. In a simple DC motor, a split-ring commutator reverses coil current every half-turn so the torque continues in the same rotational sense.

13380.title: Electric Charge
13380.heading: Electric Charge
13380.content: Electric charge is a fundamental property that occurs in positive and negative forms. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Charge is conserved and quantized in multiples of the elementary charge for ordinary isolated particles, although quarks carry fractional elementary charges within composite particles. Its SI unit is the coulomb.

13383.title: Electric Current
13383.heading: Electric Current
13383.content: Electric current is the rate of charge flow, $I=dQ/dt$. Conventional current follows the direction a positive charge would move, which is opposite electron drift in a metal. In a conductor, current also depends on charge-carrier density, carrier charge, cross-sectional area, and drift speed.

13389.heading: Elastic Stream Scaling
13389.content:
Elastic stream scaling changes the resources assigned to streaming operators as event rates rise or fall. Partitioned operators can add workers during a burst and release them when demand subsides.

Moving state and repartitioning keys take time and can disrupt ordering, so a controller should react early enough to prevent queues without oscillating after every short fluctuation.

13392.title: Elaboration Stage
13392.heading: Elaboration Stage
13392.content:
The elaboration stage is the longest design stage, during which a team adds most details and refines the game through prototypes, documentation, and playtesting. Abstract intentions become specific rules, interfaces, content requirements, and production plans.

The stage is iterative rather than a single pass. Evidence from playable versions can revise details until the schedule requires [[Feature Lock]] and movement into the [[Tuning Stage]].

13395.title: Eisenstein Criterion
13395.heading: Eisenstein Criterion
13395.content:
Eisenstein's criterion proves an integer polynomial irreducible over the rationals when a prime divides every nonleading coefficient, does not divide the leading coefficient, and its square does not divide the constant term.

A change of variable can sometimes place a polynomial into a form where the criterion applies.

13398.title: Eigenvector
13398.heading: Eigenvector
13398.content:
An eigenvector of a matrix is a nonzero [[Vector]] whose direction is unchanged by multiplication with that matrix. The result equals the original vector multiplied by a scalar called its [[Eigenvalue]].

When PageRank converges, multiplying the final [[PageRank Vector]] by the Google matrix returns the same vector. It is therefore the matrix's leading eigenvector with eigenvalue one.

For a chosen eigenvalue $\lambda$, eigenvectors are the nonzero solutions of the [[Homogeneous Linear System]] $(A-\lambda I)x=0$. Together with the zero vector they form the corresponding [[Eigenspace]], so every nonzero scalar multiple is also an eigenvector.

13401.title: Eigenvalue
13401.heading: Eigenvalue
13401.content:
An eigenvalue is the scalar by which an [[Eigenvector]] is multiplied when a particular [[Matrix]] acts on it. The vector preserves its direction while its magnitude is scaled by this value.

The stable PageRank vector has eigenvalue one under the Google matrix because one more multiplication leaves it unchanged. The [[Power Method]] finds this leading eigenvector through repeated multiplication.

For a square matrix $A$, possible eigenvalues are the roots of the [[Characteristic Equation]] $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. Their sum equals the [[Matrix Trace]] and their product is related to the [[Determinant]], counted with multiplicity.

13404.title: Eigenvalue Problem
13404.heading: Eigenvalue Problem
13404.content:
An eigenvalue problem seeks a nonzero vector $x$ and scalar $\lambda$ satisfying $Ax=\lambda x$. The matrix transformation changes the vector's magnitude or sign but not its line of direction.

Rearranging gives $(A-\lambda I)x=0$. Nontrivial solutions occur only for roots of the [[Characteristic Equation]], and their vectors form an [[Eigenspace]].

Finite element vibration and waveguide analyses produce generalized eigenvalue problems. The eigenvalues represent quantities such as squared natural frequency or cutoff parameter, while eigenvectors approximate mode shapes or field distributions.

13407.title: Eigenspace
13407.heading: Eigenspace
13407.content:
The eigenspace associated with an eigenvalue $\lambda$ is the solution space of $(A-\lambda I)x=0$. It contains the zero vector and every eigenvector associated with $\lambda$.

Because it is the null space of a matrix, it is a [[Vector Subspace]]. A basis for the eigenspace describes all eigenvectors for that eigenvalue without listing infinitely many scalar multiples.

13410.title: Egonet Feature
13410.heading: Egonet Feature
13410.content:
An egonet feature is computed from the subgraph induced by a focal node, its neighbors, and the edges among them. Counts of nodes, internal edges, boundary edges, and local density summarize the focal node's social or structural environment.

Egonets balance interpretability with more context than degree alone. Anomalous relationships among egonet measures can also reveal unusual nodes or local structures.

13413.heading: Egocentric Social Bot Detection

Egocentric social bot detection represents an account together with its immediate social neighborhood. Features describe the focal user, nearby accounts, and the connections or interactions among them.

The local network supplies context for otherwise ambiguous behavior. Its usefulness depends on the availability and authenticity of neighbor data, which adversaries may also manipulate.

13416.heading: Effective Properties of Material Mixtures
13416.content:
When a mixture's measured thermal property is unavailable, a rule of mixtures can estimate it from constituent properties and mass fractions. This approximation is most defensible when the components are distributed finely enough that a representative sample has consistent composition.

Homogeneous, inhomogeneous, and heterogeneous materials do not justify the same averaging assumptions. Resolved layers or inclusions may be necessary when local paths dominate [[Fourier Heat Conduction Law|conduction]], while an effective property may suffice at scales much larger than the mixture structure.

13419.content:
Effective JPEG quality describes the compression level implied by a region's surviving quantization and distortion rather than merely the quality setting of the current file. A pasted element may have been saved earlier at a lower quality than the background before the combined image was encoded again.

Recompression probes compare how regions change under candidate qualities to estimate this hidden history. Quality numbers are encoder-dependent, so the inference is comparative: the important observation is a spatial inconsistency, not an absolute universal scale.

13422.title: Effect Size
13422.heading: Effect Size
13422.content:
An effect size quantifies the magnitude of a difference or relationship independently of the sample's p-value. It may be expressed as a standardized mean difference, a raw mean difference, a difference in proportions, a correlation, or a model-specific measure.

Power calculations require an assumed effect size because a study cannot be sized for significance in the abstract. Plausible values should come from scientific relevance, prior evidence, or a transparent sensitivity range rather than from the observed study result alone.

In the source's two-group examples, the raw difference in sample means is the observed effect. Reporting it with a [[Confidence Interval]] prevents a small p-value from being mistaken for a scientifically important result when a large sample detects a negligible difference.

13425.title: EF Core Transactions
13425.heading: EF Core Transactions
13425.content:
A database transaction groups operations so they either succeed as a unit or are rolled back together. EF Core applies transactional behavior when saving a compatible group of changes and also permits explicit transaction control for broader workflows.

Transactions protect consistency, but long-running transactions hold resources and can increase contention. A transaction boundary should therefore contain the smallest coherent business operation and define how failures are surfaced or retried.

A database transaction is expected to be atomic, consistent, isolated, and durable: its grouped statements succeed as a unit, move data between valid states, avoid unsafe interference, and persist once committed. ADO.NET exposes explicit provider transactions for operations below an ORM boundary.

13434.content:
EF Core conventions infer a database model from ordinary .NET types. Names and type patterns can identify entity keys, required or optional properties, relationships, and table mappings without configuration for every detail.

Conventions reduce repetitive mapping, while data annotations and the Fluent API override them when the inferred model does not match the intended schema. Understanding the defaults is important because an apparently small class change can alter the resulting model.

13440.title: EF Core Entity Loading Patterns
13440.heading: EF Core Entity Loading Patterns
13440.content:
EF Core can load related entities eagerly, explicitly, or lazily. Eager loading requests relationships as part of the original query, explicit loading asks for them later through the context, and lazy loading defers access until a navigation property is used.

Each pattern trades convenience against visibility and database traffic. Deliberate loading makes query costs easier to reason about, while careless lazy loading can produce many unnoticed database round trips.

13455.fileName: EF Core Change Tracking and Persistence.md
13455.title: EF Core Change Tracking and Persistence
13455.heading: EF Core Change Tracking and Persistence
13455.content:
An EF Core context tracks the state of entity instances as unchanged, added, modified, or deleted. Property changes and relationship changes become a set of database commands when `SaveChanges` or its asynchronous counterpart is called.

Tracking supports convenient unit-of-work behavior, but it consumes memory and can preserve stale state in a long-lived context. Read-only queries can disable tracking when entity updates are not needed.

Entity Framework tracks materialized entities so changes can later be translated into insert, update, or delete commands when `SaveChanges` or its asynchronous form executes. Tracking connects object mutation to persistence but also creates a defined context lifetime and state boundary.

13464.title: EDSAC
13464.heading: EDSAC
13464.content:
EDSAC was a practical stored-program computer completed under Maurice Wilkes at Cambridge in 1949. Unlike an experimental demonstration, it became a useful scientific computing service for university researchers.

Its routine operation helped establish libraries of reusable program routines and a disciplined approach to programming. EDSAC showed how stored programs could support a continuing community of users.

13470.title: Edible Scaffold
13470.heading: Edible Scaffold
13470.content:
An edible scaffold supports cultured food cells during growth and becomes part of the finished product. Gelatin fibers, textured soy protein, or other food-safe materials can provide attachment, alignment, texture, and nutrition.

Keeping the scaffold eliminates a separation step, but its flavor, cooking response, digestibility, mechanical behavior, and regulatory status must suit the food.

13473.title: Edge
13473.heading: Edge
13473.content:
An edge is a connection between vertices in a [[Graph]]. It can represent a bridge, relationship, hyperlink, dependency, possible move, or any other relation retained by the graph model.

Edges may be undirected, directed, repeated in a [[Multigraph]], or assigned numerical values in a [[Weighted Graph]]. A sequence of connected edges forms a [[Graph Path]], and many graph algorithms operate by deciding which edges to traverse or select.

13476.title: Edge Coloring
13476.heading: Edge Coloring
13476.content:
Edge coloring assigns colors to a graph's edges so that no two edges sharing a vertex have the same color. In tournament scheduling, vertices represent players, edges represent matches, and each color represents a day; the constraint prevents a player from being scheduled twice on one day.

The smallest number of colors required is the [[Chromatic Index]]. A greedy procedure can color edges efficiently, though its result depends on processing order and may use more colors than an optimal solution.

13479.title: Edge Analytics
13479.heading: Edge Analytics
13479.content:
Edge analytics performs filtering, summarization, inference, or event detection near the sensors that generate data. It reduces network traffic and can produce a response even when connectivity to a central data center is slow or unavailable.

The edge has limited power, memory, and compute capacity, so models and state must be chosen for constrained execution and coordinated with downstream analysis.

13481.heading: Document

13482.sourceSearchName: economy of mechanism economy of mechanism
13482.title: Economy of Mechanism
13482.heading: Economy of Mechanism
13482.content:
Economy of mechanism is the security principle that a design should remain as small and simple as practical. Fewer mechanisms and interactions make behavior easier to understand, test, and review.

Complexity creates places for defects and hidden assumptions to accumulate. Simplicity does not mean omitting necessary controls; it means avoiding needless machinery that enlarges the attack and failure surface.

13485.title: Economic Stagnation
13485.heading: Economic Stagnation
13485.content:
Economic stagnation occurs when too little currency or resource flows through a game economy. Scarce income, high maintenance costs, or excessive caution make players hoard rather than exchange, so the economic loop stops functioning.

Stagnation can result from overcorrecting for [[Economic Inflation]]. A healthy [[Game Economy]] needs enough gradient for both parties to perceive gain and enough liquidity for interactions to continue.

13488.title: Economic Inflation
13488.heading: Economic Inflation
13488.content:
Economic inflation in a game occurs when resources enter an economy faster than meaningful sinks remove them. Players accumulate more currency or goods than they can use, so each unit loses perceived value.

Rising rewards can create a temporary sense of power, but they remain engaging only while new spending choices matter. Balancing sources and sinks, controlling [[Arbitrage]], and providing durable uses for value limit runaway inflation.

13491.title: Echo Bot
13491.heading: Echo Bot
13491.content:
An echo bot replies with the text it receives, making it a minimal end-to-end test of bot hosting and message transport. The template proves that the endpoint, adapter, activity handler, and emulator can exchange messages before language behavior is added.

The book first special-cases a greeting and later replaces that rule with intent recognition and an intent-response map. This progression keeps infrastructure verification separate from conversational sophistication.

The energy-minimizing setting depends on whether reduced power outweighs the extra runtime. Parallel configurations should therefore be compared by both completion time and total energy.

13512.heading: Dynamic Time Warping
13512.content:
Dynamic time warping aligns two time sequences that express a similar pattern at different speeds. Early speech recognizers used it to compare an input word against stored acoustic templates despite differences in speaking rate.

Template matching worked best for small, often speaker-dependent vocabularies. Statistical sequence models such as the [[Hidden Markov Model]] later provided a more scalable treatment of variation.

13515.heading: Dynamic Time Warping Classification
13515.content:
Dynamic time warping classification compares two sequences after finding a low-cost alignment that may stretch or compress their time axes. Dynamic programming accumulates local matching costs subject to monotone path constraints.

The resulting distance lets similar shapes match despite different speeds. Broad warping windows increase flexibility and computation but can align unrelated events, so constraints often limit how far the path may depart from the diagonal.

13524.content:
Dynamic LINQ constructs query operations such as ordering from runtime strings rather than fixed source expressions. This is useful when a client chooses a sort field that is not known until the request arrives.

The flexibility also creates risk. An API should validate a requested property against its permitted model fields and supply values separately instead of accepting an unchecked expression that could contribute to [[SQL Injection]].

13527.title: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment
13527.heading: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment
13527.content:
Dynamic difficulty adjustment changes rules or resources in response to the player's performance. It may provide more help when the player struggles or increase resistance when the player succeeds, with the aim of keeping the experience near a desired [[Flow|flow state]].

Subtle adjustment can prevent prolonged boredom or frustration. Strong adjustment can make the system feel unstable or "mushy," because the apparent structure changes whenever the player pushes against it and mastery becomes harder to evaluate.

Dynamic adjustment can respond to differences in native talent, prior experience, and current performance without requiring the player to select a fixed difficulty mode. It also requires substantial testing, and familiar selectable modes may remain useful when the team cannot build a trustworthy adaptive system.

13530.heading: Dynamic Collision Sweep
13530.content:
A dynamic collision sweep accounts for object motion across a time interval by testing a shape along its displacement rather than only at its starting and ending positions. It reduces tunneling when fast objects cross thin obstacles between frames.

Relative motion can turn a moving-versus-moving query into one shape swept against another. The earliest valid time of impact identifies where response should begin before the remaining motion is considered.

13533.title: Dynamic and Kinematic Viscosity Units
13533.heading: Dynamic and Kinematic Viscosity Units
13533.content:
The book gives dynamic and kinematic viscosity separate conversion categories because their unit dimensions differ. Dynamic viscosity is represented by centipoise or millipascal seconds, while kinematic viscosity is represented by centistokes or square millimeters per second. Its examples happen to have a factor of one between the listed pairs, but that numerical coincidence does not make the two kinds of viscosity interchangeable. The unit expression identifies which conversion category and target unit are appropriate. See [[Algebraic SI Derived Units]].

Dynamic viscosity also measures a fluid's resistance to shear: a larger shear stress is required to maintain the same velocity gradient in a more viscous fluid. Kinematic viscosity divides dynamic viscosity by density, so it describes momentum diffusion rather than shear resistance alone.

13536.title: Dynamic Blender Panel Drawing
13536.heading: Dynamic Blender Panel Drawing
13536.content:
Blender calls a panel's `draw` method repeatedly as the interface updates, so its layout can respond to current state. A viewport-overlay panel can show a play-style action when drawing is disabled and a pause-style action when the handler is active.

Dynamic drawing can also conditionally reveal controls, labels, and icons without permanently rebuilding the panel class. The method should read authoritative scene or window state each time rather than relying on a visual assumption, ensuring that the controls describe what execution will actually do.

13545.heading: Dual Point Clouds
13545.content:
Correspondence analysis treats rows and columns as linked point clouds rather than analyzing one side and discarding the other. An observation is located in relation to the attributes it contains, and an attribute is located in relation to the observations in which it occurs.

The book describes transition formulas between these dual factor spaces. In a scene-word analysis, the map can therefore show scene-to-scene, word-to-word, and scene-to-word relationships. This duality is what makes the factor map a semantic context for the entire cross-tabulation.

13548.heading: Dual-Use GPS Governance
13548.content: Dual-use GPS governance balances a military need for protected, high-integrity positioning with civilian dependence on an open global utility. Operational responsibility remained with the Air Force, while national oversight evolved toward a civil-military executive committee with Defense and Transportation leadership. Decisions about degradation, signal access, funding, and interference cannot be purely technical because denying an adversary may also disrupt aviation, communications, commerce, and foreign users.

13551.title: Dual Faces of Computational Thinking
13551.heading: Dual Faces of Computational Thinking
13551.content:
Computational thinking has a backward-looking face and a forward-looking face. The first explains how machines, algorithms, and software work; the second designs new systems that answer human purposes and concerns.

The two faces reinforce one another. Understanding mechanisms makes designs feasible, while attention to use exposes what a technically correct computation must accomplish beyond merely executing its instructions.

13554.title: DRUSS Objectives
13554.heading: DRUSS Objectives
13554.content:
The DRUSS objectives define production software as dependable, reliable, usable, safe, and secure. They broaden success beyond functional correctness to include continuity of service, predictable behavior, human use, prevention of harm, and resistance to misuse.

These properties interact and can conflict. Meeting them requires architectural principles, empirical testing, human-centered evaluation, and operational monitoring rather than a single proof or development technique.

13557.heading: Drug Utilization Analytics
13557.content:
Drug utilization analytics examines prescribing, dispensing, consumption, cost, and outcomes to evaluate how medicines are used. Large healthcare datasets can reveal repeated patterns across institutions and populations.

The analysis can support efficiency and management, but codes and clinical context must be reconciled before comparisons are credible. Commercial sensitivity and patient privacy also affect access to the underlying records.

13560.title: Drone Roll, Pitch, and Yaw Control
13560.heading: Drone Roll, Pitch, and Yaw Control
13560.content: Roll and pitch arise when rotor thrust is made unequal across the corresponding body axes, tilting the total thrust vector. Yaw arises from an imbalance in the opposing rotor reaction torques. Horizontal acceleration requires a deliberate tilt so part of thrust acts sideways, followed by an opposite tilt as the vehicle approaches the desired position.

13563.heading: Drone Rotation Matrices
13563.content: Rotation matrices express a drone's orientation by transforming vectors between body-fixed and space-fixed coordinate frames. Successive rotations about axes are order-dependent, so roll, pitch, and yaw cannot be combined as ordinary scalar addition. Their time derivatives support calculation of angular velocity for control and state estimation.
